objectives: Describe the 2015, 2016 and 2022 attacks on the Ukrainian power grid in the right order
Explain the difference between hijacking an operator's HMI and sending protocol commands directly
Map the key steps to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS techniques
Relate the attacks to the password, Flood & Overwrite and MitM challenges on CybICS
takeaways: In 2015 the attackers used stolen accounts, a VPN without a second factor and the operators' own HMIs to switch off power.
Industroyer (2016) and Industroyer2 (2022) automated the attack by speaking grid protocols such as IEC 104 directly.
Grid protocols, like Modbus, accept commands from anyone who can reach the device.
The attackers also targeted recovery: wiped computers and broken converters kept operators blind and forced manual work.
Being able to run the process by hand is a defence in its own right.

checkpoints.question: Industroyer sent IEC 104 commands straight to substation equipment. Which CybICS action is the closest parallel?
options: Logging in to the FUXA HMI with a guessed password
Writing a Modbus register on port 502 directly
Sitting between the HMI and the PLC as a MitM
checkpoints.explanation: Writing Modbus values directly to the PLC skips the HMI, just as Industroyer skipped the operators' screens and talked to the equipment itself. Logging in to FUXA is the 2015 method: acting through the operator's own tool. A MitM changes messages that someone else sends, while Industroyer sent its own commands.

quiz.question: How did the 2015 attackers open the breakers?
options: With custom malware that spoke IEC 104
Through the operators' own HMIs, remotely
By flooding the substation networks with traffic
With BlackEnergy 3 sending breaker commands
quiz.explanation: In 2015 the attackers used valid accounts and remote access to click through the operators' HMIs (T0859, T0823). BlackEnergy 3 was how they got into the office network months earlier, not what opened the breakers, and malware that speaks grid protocols only came in 2016 with Industroyer.

quiz.question: Why could Industroyer's commands switch breakers even though they did not come from the control centre?
options: IEC 104 does not check who sent a command
The attackers had broken IEC 104's encryption
The commands carried a stolen operator password
The commands were signed with a stolen certificate
quiz.explanation: IEC 104, like Modbus, trusts any well-formed message. There was no encryption to break, no password in the message and no signature to forge, which is exactly why reaching the device was enough. Stolen passwords mattered in 2015, when the attackers logged in to the HMIs.

quiz.question: Which steps of the 2015 attack made recovery harder? (Select all that apply)
options: Wiping computers with KillDisk
Loading broken firmware onto serial-to-Ethernet converters
Flooding the customer call centre
Logging in over the VPN with stolen passwords
quiz.explanation: Wiping, bricking the converters and flooding the call centre all hampered the response. The VPN login with stolen passwords was how the attackers reached the control network, a step towards the outage, not part of the attack on recovery.

quiz.question: Which single control would most directly have blocked the 2015 attackers' path into the control network?
options: Multi-factor authentication on the VPN
Encrypting the IEC 104 traffic
An IDS watching the control network
Keeping offline backups of converter firmware
quiz.explanation: The attackers entered with stolen passwords over a VPN without a second factor; a second factor would have stopped the stolen passwords from being enough. An IDS can notice the intrusion but does not block it, offline firmware backups speed up recovery rather than keeping anyone out, and encrypting IEC 104 would not have helped because they used the operators' own tools.

quiz.question: What happened to Industroyer2 in April 2022?
options: It caused a blackout across Kyiv
It was found and stopped before any outage
It only ran in a lab and was never deployed
It disabled the protection relays at substations
quiz.explanation: CERT-UA and ESET found Industroyer2 on the target network and prevented the planned outage. The Kyiv blackout was the 2016 attack with the first Industroyer, and the attempt to disable SIPROTEC protection relays belonged to 2016 as well, where it failed.
